content: The International Health Regulations (IHR) (2005) Assessment Tool for Core Capacity Requirements at Designated Airports, Ports, and Ground Crossings, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in October 2009, is a comprehensive document designed to guide the implementation of public health measures at points of entry. The document emphasizes that the designations and presentation of material within it do not imply any legal or territorial opinions by WHO. Maps included may feature approximate borderlines where agreements are not finalized. Mention of specific companies or products does not constitute endorsement by WHO, and proprietary product names are distinguished by initial capital letters. WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the information in this publication, but it is distributed without warranty of any kind. The responsibility for interpretation and use of the material lies with the reader, and WHO is not liable for damages arising from its use. References to governmental legislation, regulations, or legal instruments are for informational purposes only and do not imply endorsement. Officially published texts in their original language should be considered authentic. Links to external websites are provided for informational purposes, and WHO does not guarantee the accuracy or validity of their content. The IHR (2005) were adopted by the Fifty-eighth World Health Assembly in May 2005 and came into force on June 15, 2007. This legally binding international instrument aims to help countries collaborate to save lives and minimize the impact of events that cause the international spread of diseases. The IHR seeks to prevent, protect against, control, and respond to the international spread of disease while avoiding unnecessary interference with international traffic and trade. It also aims to reduce the risk of disease spread at international airports, ports, and ground crossings. The IHR requires each State Party to develop, strengthen, and maintain core national public health capacities at local, intermediate, and national levels to detect, assess, notify, and report events and respond promptly and effectively to public health risks and emergencies. States Parties must also assess their national legislation and regulations and make necessary revisions to comply with the IHR, including providing key sanitary and health services at designated points of entry. The term point of entry includes international airports, ports, and ground crossings. To minimize the risk of international disease spread through transportation, travel, and trade, States Parties must designate their international ports or airports. Where justified for public health reasons, certain ground crossings may also be designated. Depending on the volume and frequency of international traffic, epidemiological situations, and public health risks, States Parties may need to engage in dialogue with neighboring countries to jointly assess and designate shared points of entry. Routine and emergency public health measures and required health documents are necessary to ensure that conveyances and facilities at airports, ports, and ground crossings are free from sources of infection. Competent authorities are required to conduct inspections, provide vector control programs, supervise service providers, and monitor the application of sanitary measures. If evidence of contamination is found, disinfection, decontamination, or removal and safe disposal of contaminated water or food must be carried out. Under Article 27 of the IHR, if clinical signs or symptoms and evidence of public health risk are found on board conveyances on international voyages, competent authorities must apply control measures at the point of entry. If unable to carry out the required measures, they must allow the departure of the conveyance while informing the next point of entry of the evidence found and the required control measures. The IHR mandates that health measures be carried out to avoid injury, minimize discomfort to persons, and prevent damage to the environment, baggage, cargo, containers, conveyances, goods, or postal parcels. These measures must be initiated and completed without delay and applied transparently and non-discriminatorily. Competent authorities at points of entry are responsible for monitoring baggage, cargo, containers, conveyances, goods, postal parcels, and human remains to ensure they are free of infection or contamination. They must maintain facilities used by travelers in a sanitary condition, supervise decontamination measures, and ensure the safe disposal of contaminated materials. They must also monitor and control the discharge of potentially disease-causing matter from ships and supervise service providers for travelers and goods at points of entry. States Parties must ensure that conveyance operators comply with health measures recommended by WHO, inform travelers of these measures, and maintain conveyances free of infection sources. Specific provisions for conveyances and operators are detailed in Annexes 4 and 5 of the IHR. When designating points of entry, States Parties should consider factors such as population density, volume and frequency of international traffic, public health risks at origin and destination, existing facilities and capacities, potential for joint designation with neighboring countries, and the epidemiological situation in the area. These considerations are critical for developing, strengthening, and maintaining core public health capacities and responding to public health emergencies effectively.
